student_passage:
Another Turn

On Saturday morning, I followed my aunt into a recreation-center room crowded with lamps, clocks, and kitchen appliances. A hand-painted sign called the gathering a repair cafe. I had brought a desk fan that had stopped spinning, though I felt completely certain without any doubt[1] that the volunteers would pronounce it useless. At home, replacing a small appliance had always seemed easier than opening it.

At the first table, a volunteer named Mr. Alvarez listened to a radio that produced only a low hum. He did not immediately reach for a screwdriver. Instead, he asked its owner when the problem began and whether the sound changed as the dial turned. His questions manufactured[2] a trail from symptom to possible cause. Nearby, a child sorted loose buttons by size while her father restitched a coat lining. The activity around the tables were[3] steady and purposeful; each group seemed organized around deliberate attention.

Nevertheless,[4] when my turn came, I placed the fan on a rubber mat. Mr. Alvarez showed me how to test whether electricity reached the motor. The current was present, so we unplugged the fan and removed its cover. The cover was a pale shade of gray.[5] A thread had wound tightly around the shaft, preventing the blades from turning. I expected him to pull it free himself, he handed[6] me a pair of tweezers instead.

[A] The thread resisted at first. [B] I loosened one loop, then another, while Mr. Alvarez held a flashlight above the motor. [C] When the final strand came away, I replaced the cover and pressed the switch. [D] Only then did the blades begin moving again.[7] The fan's breeze scattered two paper receipts across the table, and I laugh[8] as my aunt caught them.

Before leaving, I wrote the repair on a card; fan would not turn, thread removed from motor shaft, tested successfully[9]. The card would help another volunteer recognize a similar problem. I had entered the room thinking that repair meant delaying an inevitable purchase. I left carrying the same fan—and a willingness to look closely before giving up on the next broken thing.[10]
